paragraphs.heading: A calendar for Earth
paragraphs.text: The geologic time scale is the system that splits Earth's past into standard blocks of time. It is a way of picturing deep time, built on events across Earth's history, which spans about 4.54 ± 0.05 billion years. Geologists, paleontologists, geochemists and other Earth scientists use it to say when things happened and how past events relate to each other.

paragraphs.heading: Order and dates
paragraphs.text: The scale joins two kinds of work. Chronostratigraphy sorts the rocks of Earth's crust into groups by their relative age, so that one group holds every rock laid down anywhere during a given stretch of time. Geochronology is the study of geological time itself. It measures ages with methods such as radiometric dating, and uses relative tools like paleomagnetism and stable isotope ratios to build a timeline. Together they put rock sequences in order and fix dates on the boundaries between them.

paragraphs.heading: Reading the layers
paragraphs.text: A few simple rules show which rocks are older. In layers that have not been disturbed, the oldest lie at the bottom and newer ones stack on top; this is the law of superposition. A rock that cuts across another must be younger than the rock it cuts, and bits of one rock caught inside another must have formed first. By the principle of faunal succession, distinct sets of fossils follow one another up through the layers in a fixed, reliable order. That lets geologists match up layers even where they are not continuous.

paragraphs.heading: Rocks and time
paragraphs.text: Each body of rock has a matching span of time. All the rocks of the Silurian System, for instance, were laid down during the Silurian Period. Better dating can change the age given to a span of time without moving its boundary in the rocks. Ages are given in Ma, short for megaannum, or million years. In early 2022 the start of the Cambrian Period was revised from 541 Ma to 538.8 Ma, yet the rock boundary between the Ediacaran and Cambrian stayed where it was.

paragraphs.heading: Golden spikes
paragraphs.text: The International Commission on Stratigraphy, part of the International Union of Geological Sciences, sets the official units. A Global Boundary Stratotype Section and Point, or GSSP, informally called a golden spike, is a precise point in a particular rock sequence, at a named place, where a stage begins. Beds above the spike belong to one interval and beds below it to another, and rocks of a similar age elsewhere can be matched to it. The base of the Paleogene, for example, is marked by the iridium anomaly left by the Chicxulub asteroid impact. Its GSSP sits at Oued Djerfane in Tunisia, but rocks carrying the anomaly turn up worldwide.

paragraphs.heading: Fixed ages and local names
paragraphs.text: Not every part of the scale is defined by rocks. Apart from the Ediacaran, the Proterozoic, along with the Archean and Hadean, is divided by set ages rather than by features in the rock. The official units are published on the International Chronostratigraphic Chart, though some regions still use local terms. The start of the Jurassic Period, given as 201.4 ± 0.2 Ma, means 201,400,000 years old, give or take 200,000 years.
